title: Sawyer v. Mills
lead: Barbara Sawyer secretly recorded lawyer Melbourne Mills agreeing to a large bonus in monthly installments after she helped develop his mass-tort practice. Although a jury awarded the unpaid balance, Kentucky’s courts held the promise unenforceable because of its terms, past services, lack of a signed memorandum, and deficient reliance evidence.

actors.name: Barbara Sawyer
actors.role: Worker who helped develop mass-tort business and sought an unpaid bonus.

actors.name: Melbourne Mills
actors.role: Lawyer who made the disputed bonus promise.

actors.name: Justice Noble
actors.role: Author of the unanimous Kentucky Supreme Court opinion.

proceedings: Jury awarded Sawyer $900,000. Trial court entered judgment notwithstanding the verdict for Mills; Court of Appeals and Kentucky Supreme Court affirmed. Prejudgment interest was not decided.
limits: The account follows the consistent March 31, 2002 termination and nine-month chronology rather than an isolated conflicting source date. The court did not decide a universal estoppel exception or categorically reject knowingly adopted recorded contracts.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Sawyer helps build the practice before the disputed promise
sections.cue: Earlier compensation and benefits are separate from the later bonus.
paragraphs: Barbara Sawyer met lawyer Melbourne Mills in 1991 and later helped his practice obtain mass-tort clients. In 1994 she asked him to join already pending breast-implant class litigation and solicited women she knew. Mills promised a large bonus if one of his class actions produced a substantial payday. From 1994 through 2001, Sawyer performed marketing and research, worked briefly as a contract employee, and received compensation. In 1997 she suggested and helped publicize Fen-Phen litigation; about 2,600 claimants responded, including four hundred in Kentucky, and she helped with ensuing office work. Earlier benefits included advertising payments, a studio payment, and vacations.

After the Fen-Phen settlement in May 2001 and receipt of fees in June, Mills gave substantial bonuses to several employees. Sawyer initially received approximately $1,300, equivalent to two weeks of hourly compensation. On June 25, she and her husband invited Mills to their art studio and secretly recorded the conversation.

sections.title: The proposed bonus is payable over years
sections.cue: Partial payment does not produce a signed memorialization.
paragraphs: Sawyer proposed $1,065,000: $1 million plus $65,000 for a car. Mills could afford a lump sum but rejected immediate payment, expressing concern that other employees would learn of the larger bonus. He agreed to monthly payments of $10,000. A lawyer later prepared a written memorialization, but Mills never signed it.

Periodic payments, including $10,000 on June 25, totaled $65,000. Mills separately paid $100,000 in October. The last payment occurred in February 2002; Sawyer’s employment ended March 31, 2002. She had received $165,000 toward the proposed bonus. The services invoked to justify it had already been completed before June 25. Her later hourly work was separately compensated.

The trial court denied summary judgment to permit development of the evidence. After four days of trial, the jury found an agreement capable of completion within one year and awarded the unpaid $900,000. The court then entered judgment notwithstanding the verdict under the statute of frauds. The Court of Appeals affirmed, and Kentucky’s Supreme Court accepted discretionary review.

sections.title: The actual installment agreement cannot be replaced by hypothetical early payment
sections.cue: Past work also fails as performance of the later promise.
paragraphs: Justice Noble wrote for a unanimous court. Evidence had to be viewed favorably to the verdict winner, with judgment notwithstanding the verdict appropriate only when a reasonable person could not find for that party. Nevertheless, the terms the parties adopted controlled.

Kentucky Revised Statutes 371.010(7) requires a signed writing for an agreement not to be performed within one year. An agreement capable of performance within a year may escape that requirement, but Sawyer could not substitute imagined lump-sum payment for the actual arrangement. Mills expressly rejected it, and the conversation repeatedly contemplated years of installments. The proposed writing specified 107 monthly installments with the last adjusted to the balance; conversational references to ten years did not establish 120 full payments. Mills’s financial ability to choose different terms did not make these terms performable within a year.

Sawyer’s full-performance argument also failed. The relevant work preceded the June promise and therefore was neither performance of that agreement nor consideration for it. Cases involving a promise in return for future requested services were different. Continued employment was separately paid and was not shown to condition the bonus. The past-services defect supplied an additional ground distinct from the missing writing.

sections.title: A recorded voice is not necessarily an electronic signature
sections.cue: Neither the secret tape nor the checks supplies the required memorandum.
paragraphs: The federal Electronic Signatures in Global and National Commerce Act did not make the conversation a signed contract. The tape was an electronic record under 15 U.S.C. §7006(4), but an electronic signature under §7006(5) requires a sound, symbol, or process adopted with intent to sign. Identifying Mills’s voice established the speaker, not intent to adopt a recording he did not know existed. The subsequent plan for a written memorialization, which he refused to sign, reinforced the distinction.

The court’s forgery analogy concerned lack of adoption; it did not decide a criminal accusation against Sawyer. Nor did the court reject all recorded agreements: parties could knowingly adopt a recording as their contract. The defect was signing intent rather than electronic form.

Calloway, a precedent involving an oral settlement entered under oath in court, rested on judicial stipulation, estoppel, and administration-of-justice considerations absent from a secret studio conversation. The signed checks also did not cure the deficiency. Cases allowing checks as memoranda involved references to contract terms or connected writings. These checks were equally consistent with a gratuitous bonus, and the unadopted recording could not supply incorporated terms. Combining the two insufficient components did not create the required signed memorandum.

sections.title: The reliance theory fails without resolving the broader doctrinal dispute
sections.cue: The defense judgment survives despite the jury’s award.
paragraphs: The parties disputed whether Sawyer preserved promissory estoppel, and Kentucky precedent left uncertainty about its ability to overcome the statute of frauds. The court distinguished promise-based reliance from equitable estoppel involving fraud, treated broad language in Rickert as dicta, and discussed differing approaches to unconscionable injury and injustice. It did not decide a universal exception. Even assuming preservation and an available exception, Sawyer lacked sufficient proof for an instruction.

A promise must induce action or forbearance the promisor should reasonably expect. Sawyer said she stayed employed and rejected other opportunities because of the bonus, but the record did not substantiate those assertions beyond her account. Nothing showed that Mills conditioned the bonus on continued work or asked her to decline other work. During roughly nine additional months she received both the $165,000 and hourly pay. The court found no basis to expect Mills to understand those circumstances as the claimed detrimental reliance.
All justices concurred in affirming the Court of Appeals and the judgment for Mills. The $900,000 verdict was not reinstated, and Sawyer’s request for prejudgment interest was not decided.
